claim: Each text cell's style is found by scanning every decoration and every search match, with a string-keyed face lookup per decoration per cell. compose is therefore O(text cells × (decorations + matches)). M0's every-match search highlight already exceeds K15's 1 ms core budget in the owner's own layout, and blows the 8.3 ms frame at 300×100. M1's syntax providers make it worse.
evidence:
scene.rs:534 `for (_, f) in deco.iter().filter(|(r, _)| r.contains(&q))`. scene.rs:535 `faces.get(f)` is a HashMap<String> lookup (faces.rs:321-328). scene.rs:538 `hl.search.iter().any(|m| m.contains(&q))`. scene.rs:553 `t.line_of(q)` runs per cell for linewise selection. All are called for every text cell (scene.rs:601). Release-mode probe (scratchpad/scene-and-unsafe/sceneprobe), p50 per compose:
- 300×100, scene.rs as it is (396 faces from a token provider): 0.48 ms.
- 300×100, dense 280-column lines: plain 0.61 ms; search "e" alone 10.2 ms; 3,703 provider faces 26.0 ms; both 36.5 ms.
- The owner's layout (an 80-column text area, 98 rows, dense wrapped text): plain 0.15 ms; search "e" 1.24 ms; token provider 1.86 ms.
V2 redraws on every keystroke of an incremental search, so `/e` is the common case. faces and scene stand at 820 of 950 lines, and the fix adds about 20.

verifier.reasoning:
The code shows it: style_at (scene.rs:532-563) scans every `deco` entry, with a HashMap<String> lookup in faces.get, and every search match, for each text cell. The reviewer understates the problem. Stored face decorations are taken from the whole buffer, not the visible range. `t.decorations()` (text.rs:610) is `self.decos.iter()`, and scene.rs:498-504 doesn't filter it. So off-screen decorations cost as much as visible ones.

My own release benchmark (scratchpad/verify-scene-and-unsafe/bench, die-core at HEAD, p50 per compose) on a 300x100 frame with dense lines:
- plain: 0.62 ms
- search "e": 29.6 ms
- 11k stored faces: 76.6 ms
- both: 105.9 ms
- about 10k stored faces, all off-screen: 72.9 ms
- an 80-column window: plain 0.16 ms, search 2.1 ms, faces 9.5 ms

I applied the reviewer's sweep, plus a visible-range clip, in a copy (scratchpad/verify-scene-and-unsafe/clean). All 28 scene tests and all 147 die-core tests pass. Times after the fix:
- 300x100: plain 0.67 ms; off-screen faces 0.67 ms; search 0.81 ms; faces 0.84 ms; both 1.00 ms.
- 80-column window: 0.18 to 0.27 ms.

The sweep as written is correct:
- `active` stays ordered by deco index, so the stacking order is unchanged.
- Empty ranges never apply.
- Search matches are sorted and don't overlap.
- It needs `q.map_or(base, &mut style_at)`, because the closure is FnMut.

Two gaps:
1. Without the clip, it still builds and sorts `layers` from every decoration in the buffer, every frame.
2. The proposed K15 test (300x100, 4000 faces and a one-letter search within 1 ms) would be flaky or fail. Plain compose is already 0.62-0.67 ms. Fixed, 'both' is 1.00 ms in release and 0.97 ms at the test profile's opt-level 1 (Cargo.toml `[profile.test] opt-level = 1`).
verifier.better_fix:
Use the reviewer's sweep, with `let style = q.map_or(base, &mut style_at);`. Also clip stored decorations to what's drawn (scene.rs:500-503):
```rust
Deco::Face(f) if d.range.start < visible.end && d.range.end > visible.start => {
    Some((d.range.clone(), f))
}
```
Keep the proptest oracle, `style_sweep_matches_the_naive_scan`. Replace the speed test with two tests:
- `an_80_column_window_with_4000_faces_and_a_one_letter_search_composes_within_1ms`: the owner's layout, measured at 0.25 ms.
- `faces_and_search_cost_at_most_twice_a_plain_frame`: 300x100 with 4000 stored faces (half of them off-screen) and the search "e", p50 of 20 runs, at most 2x the plain frame's p50. It holds at opt-level 1 and in release, and it catches a return to the per-cell scan (100x today).

This removes about 4 lines from the reviewer's estimate.

claim: Layout gives a newline no cell, so compose never draws one. A linewise (or charwise, across a newline) visual selection is invisible on empty lines, where Vim and the owner's Emacs show one highlighted cell. An empty line, and the cells past the end of any line, also map to no position, so K14's click can't land on an empty line or past the end of a line from the frame.
evidence:
Probe on "ab

cd
", visual linewise over all three lines: row 0 `##........`, row 1 `..........`, row 2 `##........`. The empty line shows no selection. positions: row 0 `[Some(0), Some(1), None × 8]`; row 1 (the empty line) all None; row 3 all None. The rustdoc (scene.rs:147-151) promises None past the end of a line. K8's selection test only checks non-empty lines (tests/scene.rs:388-425).
proposed_fix:
In draw_text, after a display row's cells, when the row ends its buffer line:
- Let `nl` be the newline's position, or the buffer's end on the last line.
- Draw the next cell (if it's inside `room`) as `Cell::new(Glyph::Char(' '), style_at(nl))`.
- Set that cell's and the rest of the row's positions to `Some((p.window, nl))`. Under scene-2 this goes into the Ctx table instead.
Rustdoc: "Cells past the end of a line map to its newline (on the last line, to the end of the buffer), so a click there lands at the line's end, as in Emacs; die-vim moves it onto the last character in normal state. The newline's own cell draws its faces, so a selected or highlighted newline shows as one cell, as in Vim."
Tests:
- `linewise_selection_shows_empty_lines`: the case above, with row 1 col 0 selected.
- `charwise_selection_across_a_newline_shows_it`.
- `cells_past_the_end_of_a_line_map_to_its_newline`.
- Update `every_cell_of_a_tab_or_wide_character_maps_to_its_position`: its last element becomes Some(6).
failing_test:
linewise_selection_shows_empty_lines: "ab

cd
", State::Visual, Selection{anchor:0, head:4, shape:Line}; assert row 1 col 0's bg is the selection face's

verifier.reasoning:
Reproduced in a probe test (scratchpad/verify-scene-and-unsafe/orig/crates/die-core/tests/probe.rs).
- "ab\n\ncd\n", visual linewise over all three lines: the selection masks are `##........`, `..........`, `##........`, so the empty line shows nothing.
- Charwise 1..=3 (b and both newlines): `.#........`, then nothing on the empty line.
- Positions: row 0 is [Some(0), Some(1), None x 8], row 1 is all None, and row 3 (the empty last line) is all None.

The cause is in layout.rs:198-205 and :272-279: the newline gets `stop_here(p)`, a stop with no cell. The rustdoc (scene.rs:147-151) does say None past the end of a line, so that half is documented behaviour, but it leaves K14 nothing to map a click to.

The one-cell rendering is consistent with the owner's Emacs. mono-dark's region (mono-dark-theme.el:37) has no :extend, so Emacs highlights only the newline glyph, which is also what Vim does.

The fix is incomplete for wrapped lines: only rows that end their buffer line get positions past their last cell. A click past the end of a non-final wrapped row still maps to None, and Emacs puts point at that row's end. The proposed rustdoc ('Cells past the end of a line map to its newline') would read as covering those rows too.
verifier.better_fix:
Take the reviewer's change for rows that end their line. Add:
- A row that doesn't end its line maps the cells past its last cell to that row's last drawn position (the break position, which die-vim's `l`/`h` rules then handle).
- Rustdoc: "Cells past the end of a row map to its last position; past the end of a line's last row, to its newline (on the last line, to the end of the buffer), so a click there lands at the line's end, as in Emacs."
- Test `cells_past_a_wrapped_row_map_to_its_last_position`.

An equivalent, and cleaner while K4 rebuilds layout: emit the end-of-line stop as a real cell (`CellKind::Eol`, text " ", pos Some(nl)) at the (row, col) that stop_here already reserves. Layout, motions and the scene then agree, and draw_text needs no special case.

claim: Cell can't yet hold what a ghostel-level terminal needs, and adding it later breaks every cell producer. It lacks overline and a link id. Nothing says producers must resolve reverse, faint and invisible themselves. Each attribute is its own public bool with no public constructor, so every new attribute breaks every struct literal once die-term (M2) and cell-writing surfaces construct cells. Surface::render still returns strings, where contract §10 has surfaces write cells into a frame. Box<str> clusters make Cell non-Copy and 40 bytes.
evidence: scene.rs:56-74 has the fields glyph, fg, bg, bold, italic, strike, underline, underline_color. `Cell::new` is private (scene.rs:78). ctx.rs:67 `fn render(&mut self, cols: usize, rows: usize, out: &mut Vec<String>)`, while contract §10 says "render writes into a DIE-owned cell frame clipped to area". S4 A5: "The spike renders strings; production renders the cell frame." ghostel's resolved cell (lisp/ghostel/src/style_face.zig:31-44): fg, bg, bold, italic, faint, underline, underline_color, strikethrough, overline, inverse, hyperlink. Faint is blended into fg at 65/35 (style_face.zig:77-89), inverse becomes :inverse-video, and blink and invisible aren't rendered. S1's cell used an `attrs: u8` bitset (spikes/s1-renderer/src/scene.rs:9-14). size_of::<Cell>() = 40, Glyph = 24.
recommendation: Use flags plus a constructor and overline now, and the link id and cell frame with die-term. Skip interning unless R2's profile asks for it.

verifier.reasoning:
scene.rs:56-74 has bold, italic and strike as separate pub bools; Cell::new (scene.rs:78) is private and takes a Style. Nothing outside die-core constructs a Cell today (grep for `Cell {` finds only scene.rs). ctx.rs:67's render takes `&mut Vec<String>`, against contract §10:321, which already says 'the link id arrives with die-term (M2)'. size_of::<Cell>() = 40, confirmed.

The proposed fix doesn't guarantee that later additions are non-breaking. A bitset plus a constructor still lets a producer write a full struct literal, and that literal breaks when a field is added. Only `#[non_exhaustive]` rules out outside literals, including functional update. Attrs(u16) also doesn't shrink Cell: it stays 40 bytes, padding included.
verifier.decision_view: Now: `#[non_exhaustive]` on Cell plus a public `Cell::new(glyph, fg, bg)`, and the rustdoc rule for reverse, faint, invisible and blink. Overline, the link id and the cell frame for surfaces then arrive with die-term in M2 without breaking anyone, so none of them needs adding now. Bools or a bitset is then just style; keep the bools, which read better in tests. Skip cluster interning unless R2's profile asks for it.

claim: The snapshot silently merges every style past the 62nd into '?', so two different styles can produce the same snapshot. The style key is a hand-written tuple, so a new Cell attribute that isn't added to it also merges styles without an error. M2's 256-colour terminal tests will pass 62 easily.
evidence: scene.rs:202 has 62 letters, and scene.rs:218 and :227 use `unwrap_or('?')`. Probe: a row of 70 distinct fg colours gives style row `|abc…XYZ0123456789????????|` and 10 legend lines starting with "? ". scene.rs:190-201 builds `key` field by field.
proposed_fix: Write `let Cell { glyph: _, fg, bg, bold, italic, strike, underline, underline_color } = c;` (an exhaustive destructure, so a new field fails to compile here until the key and legend include it). Replace the two `unwrap_or('?')` with `*letters.get(i).unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("a snapshot shows at most {} styles", letters.len()))`. If M2 needs more, go to two-character keys then. New attributes print only when set, so existing snapshots stay valid. Test: `a_snapshot_with_more_styles_than_letters_panics`.

Two scenes with 62 distinct styles in cols 0-61, then X, Y at 62-63, and col 64 = X in one and Y in the other. They give byte-identical snapshot() strings while `s == t` is false, because the style row reads `???` in both and the legend lists X then Y in both. claim: The unsafe confinement can be bypassed three ways that every ci check accepts. (a) A `#[unsafe(naked)]` function with `naked_asm!` is arbitrary machine code, needs no `unsafe` block, and rustc's `unsafe_code` lint doesn't flag it, even under the workspace's `forbid`. (b) In die-render, where the level is `deny`, a macro that builds `#[allow($lint)]` lowers it, and the token lint never sees `allow(unsafe_code)`. (c) A `#[path = "…"]` module whose file is outside every workspace member is never scanned, so an inner `#![allow(unsafe_code)]` there passes.
evidence: Probe crate (scratchpad/scene-and-unsafe/probe, rustc 1.96.0, `[workspace.lints.rust] unsafe_code = "forbid"`): `#[unsafe(naked)] pub extern "C" fn f(_x: u64) -> u64 { core::arch::naked_asm!("add x0, x0, #1", "ret") }` compiles and runs (`cargo run` printed 42). The same probe shows what rustc does catch: `unsafe extern` blocks ("usage of an `unsafe extern` block"), `global_asm!`, `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]` and unsafe in build.rs ("requested on the command line with `-F unsafe-code`"). End to end, in a `git archive HEAD` copy (scratchpad/scene-and-unsafe/tree) I appended the naked fn to crates/die-core/src/lib.rs. To crates/die-render/src/lib.rs I appended `macro_rules! level { ($lint:ident, $($i:item)*) => { #[allow($lint)] pub mod planted { $($i)* } }; } level!(unsafe_code, pub fn ok() -> &'static str { unsafe { std::str::from_utf8_unchecked(b"ok") } });` and `#[path = "../../../docs/planted.rs"] pub mod planted_path;`, with docs/planted.rs holding `#![allow(unsafe_code)]` and an unsafe block. Then `cargo check -p die-core -p die-render` passed, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` exited 0, `cargo xtask lint` printed `lint: ok (7 crates)`, and `cargo xtask budget` passed. Cause: check_unsafe_allows (lint.rs:534-591) only looks for the literal tokens `allow|expect|warn(` … `unsafe_code`. rust_files scans member directories only (util.rs:204). guards.rs:12 plants only `unsafe {}`. Today's tree has no `unsafe` token outside platform/macos except inside string literals (xtask/src/guards.rs:12, lint.rs:641), and no `#[path]` or `include!` anywhere, so a stricter rule costs nothing.
failing_test: lint::tests: check_unsafe_tokens on "#[unsafe(naked)]\npub extern \"C\" fn f() { core::arch::naked_asm!(\"ret\") }\n" at crates/die-core/src/x.rs must give 1 error (today no check exists, and the full ci gauntlet passes the plant)

verifier.reasoning:
Reproduced all three bypasses myself with rustc 1.96.0, offline. (a) Probe scratchpad/verify-scene-and-unsafe/naked has `[lints.rust] unsafe_code = "forbid"` and a `#[unsafe(naked)]` fn with `naked_asm!`. `cargo run` printed 42 with no lint. claim: Face::glyph passes pointers made from references to the first element only (`&mut chars[0]`, `&mut glyphs[0]`). For a non-BMP character, Core Text then reads 2 UTF-16 units and writes 2 glyphs through them, which is out of those references' range. That is UB under Stacked Borrows (Miri's default) and accepted by Tree Borrows. Emoji, CJK Extension B and Nerd Font plane-15 icons all take this path. Nothing misbehaves today, since the access happens in C.

The objc2-core-text 0.3.2 doc for CTFontGetGlyphsForCharacters (generated/CTFont.rs:1152-1158) says `count` is "the capacity of both the characters and glyphs arrays", and non-BMP characters are surrogate pairs. Miri isn't installed, and couldn't run the FFI call anyway.

claim: The font descriptor comes from a raw-pointer dereference whose lifetime the compiler doesn't tie to `descs`. It's sound only because `desc` is used before `descs` drops. Its SAFETY comment leaves out the bounds requirement, which line 42 happens to meet, and the block holds two unsafe operations. text.rs:67 puts five calls under one SAFETY comment.

text.rs:47 `&*(descs.value_at_index(0) as *const CTFontDescriptor)` has an unbounded lifetime, and value_at_index needs the in-bounds index that line 42 happens to guarantee. Adding the two clippy lints in a copy flagged exactly text.rs:47 (2 operations) and text.rs:67 (5 operations). The placement the reviewer proposes for the lint levels fails, though. Putting `#[deny(clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks, clippy::multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block)]` on `pub mod macos` after `#[allow(unsafe_code)]` makes today's `cargo xtask lint` fail: 'platform/mod.rs:15: allow(unsafe_code) outside the modules scope §12 permits'. check_unsafe_allows compares the tokens after the allow's `]` with "pub mod macos" (lint.rs:564-579), and the extra attribute changes them. Set the levels in die-render's manifest instead, where they can't be detached from the module:
```toml
[lints.clippy]
undocumented_unsafe_blocks = "deny"
multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block = "deny"
```
I verified it: clippy then flags only metrics() once the descriptor fix is in, and `cargo xtask lint` stays ok. In lint.rs's OWN_LINTS branch, require both keys, next to the existing `unsafe_code = "deny"` check. Use the reviewer's descriptor code, and split metrics() into one `unsafe` per getter.

claim: platform/mod.rs says logic "lives outside this module and calls in". lib.rs says neutral code is what "only platform::macos calls". The first is impossible as written: neutral code can't name `platform::macos` without a `target_os` cfg, which the lint forbids in neutral code, or the Linux cross-check fails. So R2's frame driver (diff, atlas calls, instance building, encode order) would have to live in platform::macos, against the thin-wrapper rule.
evidence: platform/mod.rs:5-8: "Anything with logic of its own (the atlas, the row cache, instance building, key mapping) lives outside this module and calls in." lib.rs:10-14: "neutral code that only `platform::macos` calls is dead on Linux … Mark it `#[cfg_attr(not(target_os = \"macos\"), allow(dead_code))]`". platform/mod.rs:14-16 has `#[cfg(target_os = "macos")] pub mod macos;`. lint.rs:316-500 flags target_os cfgs outside platform/. m0-plan R2: "The test plan states the frame-data boundary between neutral code and the backend".
recommendation: The `backend` alias with a stub: the orchestration stays neutral and testable on Linux, and no traits are needed before the second implementation (platforms.md §5.2).

verifier.reasoning:
Both quotes are accurate. platform/mod.rs:5-8 says logic 'lives outside this module and calls in'. lib.rs:10-14 talks of 'neutral code that only platform::macos calls'. Neutral code can't name `platform::macos` without a target_os cfg, because the module doesn't exist on Linux and the cross-check would fail, and check_platform_code forbids that cfg outside platform/. So today the only allowed direction is platform::macos calling neutral code, which would put a frame driver inside platform. platforms.md §5.2 defers traits until the second implementation, so an alias in platform/mod.rs, where cfg is allowed, is the natural fix.

The proposed lint check, though, would flag crates/die-render/tests/platform.rs:6-7 (`use die_render::platform::macos::metal::Gpu;`). That file is in NEUTRAL's allowed list and is macOS-only. Also, `ci --linux` runs the tests in a container, so any neutral test that reaches the stub fails there.
verifier.decision_view: Take the `backend` alias with a stub that holds only the items neutral code names, with no traits. Also make R2's boundary data in and data out: neutral code (diff, atlas packing, instance building) takes rasterized glyphs and metrics as values, or through a closure, and never calls the backend itself. Only the driver calls `platform::backend`. Then neutral tests run on Linux, and driver tests stay macOS-only.
verifier.better_fix: Take the reviewer's platform/mod.rs alias and rustdoc. The lint rule ('`platform :: macos` outside crates/die-render/src/platform/ is an error') should exempt crates/die-render/tests/platform.rs, or that test should switch to `platform::backend`. Add to R2's test plan: neutral functions take glyph bitmaps and metrics as data and never call `platform::backend`, so their tests run under `ci --linux`. Rewrite lib.rs:10-14 instead of dropping it. Its `cfg_attr(…, allow(dead_code))` advice still applies to neutral code that only the macOS backend calls back into.

claim:
The module's rules don't yet cover what R3 and R4 bring:
- Rust closures that AppKit calls (the NSEvent monitor block, delegates, a display-link callback), where a panic must not unwind into Objective-C frames;
- AppKit's main-thread requirement.
Neither applies today: no Rust code is called from foreign code, and nothing touches AppKit.
evidence: appkit.rs is empty (2 comment lines). Core Text and Metal calls today need no main thread. MTLDevice is Send + Sync in objc2-metal 0.3.2, and CTFont is neither Send nor Sync (objc2-core-text 0.3.2 thread_safety.rs), so the compiler confines a Face to its thread.
proposed_fix: Add to platform/mod.rs's rustdoc: "A Rust closure that Objective-C or C calls (a block, a delegate method, a display-link callback) runs its body in `catch_unwind` and never lets a panic unwind into the framework; it logs and drops the event. AppKit calls take a `MainThreadMarker`, so they can't compile off the main thread." R3 and R4's test plans include `a_panic_in_the_key_monitor_is_caught`.

verifier.reasoning: appkit.rs is two comment lines, and no Rust code is called from foreign code today. The rule matters for R3 and R4. block2 0.6.2 invokes blocks through `extern "C-unwind"` (block2 src/abi.rs:239), so a panic in DIE's own NSEvent-monitor block would unwind through AppKit frames rather than abort. winit 0.30.13 already catches panics in its own handlers on macOS (`stop_app_on_panic` and `resume_unwind`, platform_impl/macos/event_loop.rs:439-444), so only DIE's own blocks, delegates and display-link callbacks need the rule. objc2-app-kit's MainThreadMarker requirement makes the main-thread rule checkable at compile time. The proposed rustdoc and test name are fine; mention that winit's handlers are already covered.

claim: Scope §12 implies DIE's only unsafe is in the named modules. The guard actually confines unsafe written in DIE's own source. Dependency macros expand unsafe code into DIE's crates unflagged, which is correct behaviour but should be stated so the review's scope is clear.
evidence: crates/die-core/src/ids.rs:4 uses `slotmap::new_key_type!`, which expands to `unsafe impl $crate::Key for $name` (slotmap-1.1.1/src/lib.rs:460). die-core compiles under `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, because rustc doesn't report the lint inside external macros.

Unsafe code inside dependencies, including what their macros expand to in DIE's crates (slotmap's `new_key_type!` emits an `unsafe impl Key`), belongs to the dependency and isn't part of this review."

verifier.reasoning: ids.rs:4 calls `slotmap::new_key_type!`, which expands to `unsafe impl $crate::Key for $name` (slotmap-1.1.1/src/lib.rs:460). die-core still compiles under the workspace's forbid, because rustc doesn't report unsafe_code inside external macro expansions. The token rule from unsafe-1 can't see it either, so the scope sentence is needed to set the review's boundary. Its first half depends on unsafe-1 landing. One clause worth adding: a dependency macro that wraps caller code in `unsafe` would also be invisible to both checks, so adding such a macro is a dependency-review decision.

claim: from_file turns the path into a UTF-8 string, so a font under a non-UTF-8 path fails. It also doesn't check `px`: Core Text silently uses 12 pt for 0.0.
evidence: text.rs:31-38 builds `CFString::from_str(path.to_str()…)` and then `CFURL::with_file_system_path`. objc2-core-foundation 0.3.2 has `CFURL::from_file_path(path)` (src/url.rs:88), which uses the path's bytes. The CTFontCreateWithFontDescriptor doc (generated/CTFont.rs:259): "If 0.0 is specified … the default font size of 12.0 will be used."
proposed_fix: `let url = CFURL::from_file_path(path).ok_or_else(bad)?;`, which drops the CFString step. Add `if !(px > 0.0 && px.is_finite()) { return Err(format!("font size {px} isn't a positive size")); }`.

verifier.reasoning: text.rs:31 does `path.to_str()`, then CFString, then CFURL::with_file_system_path. objc2-core-foundation 0.3.2 has `CFURL::from_file_path` (src/url.rs:88, unix, from the path's bytes). I measured px: `Face::from_file(…, 0.0)` gives ascent 11.58, the same as 12.0, so Core Text silently uses 12 pt. The fix (from_file_path plus the px check) compiles, drops the CFString and CFURLPathStyle imports, and passes the platform tests, including a new assert that px 0.0 is an error. The non-UTF-8 half is mostly theoretical on macOS, since APFS stores names as UTF-8. The px half is the useful part.
